item.title: Girl with a Pearl Earring
item.lesson: This is not a portrait. Dutch painters called this kind of picture a tronie — a study of a face in costume, sold on the open market, no sitter's name attached — which is why we will never know who she is, and why she can be anyone. Vermeer strips away everything: no room, no window, no table, just a girl turning against darkness in an 'exotic' turban of ultramarine and yellow, lips parted as if you had just said her name. The pearl is a magic trick — look closely and it is barely there, two strokes: a bright highlight and a soft reflection of her collar, floating without an earhook. The painting vanished into obscurity for two centuries and was bought at auction in 1881 for two guilders plus buyer's premium — roughly the price of a decent dinner. Restoration in 1994 recovered the luminosity that earned her the nickname 'the Mona Lisa of the North.'
item.lookFor: Find the two tiny white dots at the corners of her mouth and eyes — Vermeer's optical dew, possibly evidence of his experiments with lenses, that make the whole face seem freshly lit.
